_meta.method: original literal English gloss from the Sanskrit commentary; Sanskrit order preserved; no machine-translation prose

1.translation: At the end of the previous chapter the Lord mentioned seven subjects—Brahman, adhyātma, and the rest—and Arjuna wishes to know their truth: “What is that Brahman? What is adhyātma? What is action, O Supreme Person? What is called adhibhūta, and what is called adhidaiva?”
word_for_word: at the end of the previous chapter
of the subjects mentioned by the Lord
of the seven beginning with Brahman and adhyātma

2.translation: “Who is adhiyajña here in this body, O Madhusūdana? How does he abide in this body and preside over the sacrifice? And how are You to be known at the time of departure by people whose minds are disciplined?” Śrīdhara explains that “sacrifice” stands for all action; Arjuna asks who presides over it, impels it, and gives its fruit, and by what means that Lord is known at death.
word_for_word: who is the presiding Lord of sacrifice
by people whose minds are disciplined
is an indication of all actions

3.translation: The Blessed Lord answered in the order of the questions: “The imperishable Supreme is Brahman; one’s own nature is called adhyātma; the outpouring that causes the coming-into-being and growth of beings is called action.” Śrīdhara explains that “imperishable” means not moving or decaying; although the individual living being may also be called imperishable, the word “supreme” identifies the root cause of the world, Brahman. The Lord’s own nature becoming the living being and abiding in a body as its enjoyer is called adhyātma. “Outpouring” is sacrifice, the giving of material substance to a deity, and by extension all action that causes the origin and development of beings.
word_for_word: the root cause of the world
Brahman’s becoming in the form of the living being
presiding over the body as the Self
is called by the word adhyātma
giving material substance for a deity

4.translation: Adhibhūta is the perishable realm—the bodily and other objects that arise in relation to embodied beings. Adhidaiva is the cosmic Person, abiding in the midst of the solar orb and ruling the gods who are expressions of Him; He is the first embodied Person and the original creator. Adhiyajña is I alone, abiding as the inner controller in this body, the presiding deity of sacrifice, its impeller, and the giver of its fruit. Śrīdhara says this is understood from the Lord’s distinction from the individual living being through His detachment and other qualities.
word_for_word: arises in relation to every living being
abiding in the middle of the solar orb
the lord of all the deities
the impeller of action beginning with sacrifice
through distinction from the living being

5.translation: Śrīdhara now gives the means and result of knowing the Lord at the end of life: one who remembers Me alone, in the inner-controller form just described, and leaves the body at the time of departure, travels by the path beginning with light and reaches My state, becoming of My nature. There is no doubt here; remembrance is the means of knowledge, and attainment of My state is the result.
word_for_word: in the form of the inner controller
by the path beginning with light

6.translation: It is not only one who remembers Me who necessarily reaches My state. Whatever state—whether of another deity or something else—a person remembers when leaving the body at the end, that very state he attains, O Kaunteya. The reason is that his mind has been shaped and imbued by continually dwelling on that state.
word_for_word: remembering at the end of life
his mind shaped by that state

7.translation: Since previous impressions alone cause remembrance at the time of death, and a deliberate effort to remember is not possible then when one is helpless, remember Me and contemplate Me at all times—and fight. Constant remembrance does not arise without purification of mind, so perform your own dharma, such as battle, for that purification. With your mind and intellect offered to Me, you will reach Me alone; there is no doubt.
word_for_word: with the mind offered to Me
with the intellect offered to Me
you will come to Me alone

8.translation: The practice underlying constant remembrance is now stated: through practice-yoga, which is a continuous stream of cognitions of the same kind, and with a concentrated mind that is not inclined to go to another object, one who continually contemplates the divine, supreme Person reaches that Person, O Pārtha.
word_for_word: a continuous stream of cognitions of the same kind
not inclined to go to another object

9.translation: Śrīdhara further describes the Person to be contemplated: the omniscient one, creator of all knowledge, ancient and beginningless, the ruler and controller, subtler than the atom and subtler even than space, time, and direction; the sustainer of everything; of inconceivable form because His glory is immeasurable; beyond the reach of impure mind and intellect; self-luminous like the sun and beyond the darkness of prakṛti.
word_for_word: subtler even than space, time, and directions
beyond the reach of impure mind and intellect
self-luminous like the sun, illuminating itself and others

10.translation: At the time of departure, one who remembers this divine Supreme Person—with devotion and with an unwavering, undistracted mind—breaks through prakṛti and the body, senses, and rest. Śrīdhara explains that steadiness of mind is supported by the power of yoga: properly directing the prāṇa through the suṣumṇā path and placing it between the eyebrows. Such a person reaches that supreme Person, the luminous form of the Supreme Self.
word_for_word: having broken through prakṛti together with its manifestation
the cause of steadiness of mind
the form of the Supreme Self

11.translation: Śrīdhara now undertakes to prescribe the inward practice based on Oṃ, beyond practice-yoga alone. The imperishable syllable is what the knowers of Vedānta declare as that under whose command the sun and moon remain established. It is the state into which desireless ascetics enter and which those wishing to know it practice celibacy in the teacher’s household. “I will explain that attainable state to you briefly,” meaning that its means will now be taught.
word_for_word: the knowers of the Veda declare
under the command of this imperishable

12.translation: Śrīdhara explains the promised means together with its limbs: restrain and withdraw all the gateways of the senses, meaning do not grasp external objects through the eyes and the other senses; restrain the mind in the heart, meaning do not remember external objects; and, having placed the prāṇa in the head, at the space between the eyebrows, undertake the stability of yoga.
word_for_word: through the eyes and the like
having restrained the mind in the heart

13.translation: The one-syllable Oṃ is Brahman, either because it denotes Brahman or because it is a symbol of Brahman, like an image. Whoever utters it while remembering Me, the One it denotes, and departs after leaving the body reaches the supreme destination by the path beginning with light.
word_for_word: because it is a symbol of Brahman
by the path beginning with light

14.translation: Attainment of the Lord at the time of death through this concentration occurs through the power of continual prior practice, not for another. The person whose mind has no other object and who remembers Me continually and every day finds Me easily, O Pārtha, because he is constantly united and collected.
word_for_word: through concentration at the time of death
through the power of continual practice
whose mind has no other object

15.translation: Although the Lord is easy for such a person to attain, Śrīdhara states the result: the great souls who are My devotees reach Me and do not attain rebirth, which is impermanent and an abode of suffering. Alternatively, having attained the supreme perfection, liberation, they do not return to birth or to the dwelling-place of suffering.

16.translation: All worlds up to the world of Brahmā are subject to return, O Arjuna, because even Brahmā’s world is perishable; those who reach it without knowledge must be reborn. Śrīdhara adds that those who reach Brahmā’s world through practices leading to gradual liberation gain knowledge there and are liberated together with Brahmā, but not others. For those who reach Me, O Kaunteya, there is no rebirth.
word_for_word: the worlds up to the world of Brahmā
of those in whom knowledge has not arisen
through contemplations whose fruit is gradual liberation
those who have reached Brahmā’s world
of those in whom knowledge has arisen there

17.translation: Why are higher worlds regarded as superior if all are perishable? Śrīdhara says the distinction is their extremely long duration. Those who know through the power of yoga that Brahmā’s day lasts a thousand four-yuga cycles, and that his night lasts another thousand, are knowers of day and night. The word yuga here means a complete four-yuga cycle. A human year is a day and night of the gods; twelve thousand such divine years make a four-yuga cycle; a thousand four-yuga cycles make Brahmā’s day, and the same measure his night; one hundred such Brahmā-years make Brahmā’s full lifespan.
word_for_word: night ending after a thousand yuga-cycles
those people are knowers of day and night
a day and night of the gods
the night is of the same measure
one hundred years is Brahmā’s full lifespan

18.translation: At the arrival of Brahmā’s day, all manifest beings arise from the unmanifest, causal form; at the arrival of Brahmā’s night, they dissolve into that same causal state called the unmanifest. Śrīdhara explains that “the unmanifest” here is the causal form of the effects, from which the moving and unmoving beings become manifest.
word_for_word: the unmanifest form of the effect
having the nature of the cause
in what is called the unmanifest

19.translation: To prevent the concern that an action is destroyed without bearing fruit or that an unearned result appears, Śrīdhara shows the unbroken flow of creation and dissolution: the same multitude of moving and unmoving beings that existed before becomes manifest at the arrival of day and dissolves at the arrival of night; at the next dawn it arises again, helpless and subject to karma and the rest. No other beings arise in their place.
word_for_word: subject to karma and the rest

20.translation: Having elaborated the impermanence of the worlds, Śrīdhara now elaborates the permanence of the Supreme Lord’s nature: beyond the unmanifest that is the cause of the moving and unmoving world is another unmanifest reality, different from it, beyond the reach of the eyes and the other senses, beginningless and eternal. Even when all beings characterized by effects and causes perish, that reality does not perish.
word_for_word: the unmanifest that is the cause of the moving and unmoving
beyond the reach of the eyes and the like
in all beings characterized by effect and cause

21.translation: This reality, which is unmanifest, beyond the senses, imperishable, and free from coming into or going out of being, is called the imperishable in the Upaniṣads. The scriptures call it the supreme destination, the highest human aim: “There is nothing higher than the Person; that is the culmination, that is the supreme destination.” It is the destination from which those who attain it do not return. It is called “My abode,” meaning My own nature; thus I alone am the supreme destination.
word_for_word: free from coming into and going out of being
I alone am the supreme destination

22.translation: The supreme Person is attained only through exclusive devotion, O Pārtha—through devotion that has no other refuge. He is supreme because all beings abide within Him as their cause and because this entire world is pervaded by Him.
word_for_word: there is no other as refuge
by whom this entire world is pervaded

23.translation: The Lord has said that those who worship Him reach His state and do not return, while others return. Arjuna now asks by which path they go. Śrīdhara explains that “time” indicates the path marked by the deities presiding over its stages: on one path yogīs and worshipers go to non-return, and on the other practitioners of action go to return. “I will explain that time”—that is, that path.
word_for_word: at the time / by the path marked by that time
by deities presiding over the stages of time
who conduct the traveler along the way

24.translation: Śrīdhara now states the path of non-return. “Fire” and “light” indicate the deity presiding over the flame described in the Upaniṣads; “day” the deity presiding over the day; “bright” the deity presiding over the bright fortnight; and “the six months of the northern course” the deity presiding over the northward movement of the sun. These terms also indicate the further stages named in scripture, such as the year and the world of the gods. Those worshipers of the Lord who depart along this path reach Brahman because they are knowers of Brahman. Persons established in immediate Self-realization have no departing path, since their life-breaths do not depart.
word_for_word: fire / the deity presiding over fire
those who depart there / along that path
the year, the world of the gods, and the like
those who share in immediate liberation

25.translation: Śrīdhara states the path of return: “Smoke” indicates the deity presiding over smoke; “night,” “dark,” and “the six months of the southern course” indicate the deities presiding over night, the dark fortnight, and the sun’s southward course. A karma-yogī who departs along this path reaches the moonlight—heaven—enjoys there the fruit of iṣṭa and pūrta actions, and returns. In this way, worship combined with renunciation leads to gradual liberation; desired action leads to return after heavenly enjoyment, prohibited action to return after hellish enjoyment, and lesser actions to repeated birth here.
word_for_word: smoke / the deity presiding over smoke
the six months of the southern course
one who departs along that path
the fruit of iṣṭa and pūrta actions

26.translation: The two paths are now summarized. The bright path, beginning with flame, is luminous; the dark path, beginning with smoke, is made of darkness. These two paths are regarded as eternal and beginningless for the world, because saṃsāra is beginningless. Through the bright path one reaches non-return, liberation; through the dark path one returns again.
word_for_word: because it is made of light
because it is made of darkness

27.translation: Knowing these two paths, O Pārtha—the paths that lead to liberation and saṃsāra—no yogī is deluded. He does not desire the fruit of heaven and the like with the thought that it is happiness; rather, he remains steadfast in the Supreme Lord. Therefore, O Arjuna, be joined to yoga at all times.
word_for_word: with the thought that it is happiness
the fruit of heaven and the like

28.translation: Śrīdhara concludes the chapter and the determination of Arjuna’s eight questions: the meritorious fruit taught in the scriptures for study of the Vedas, performance of sacrifices, austerities such as mortifying the body, and gifts offered to worthy recipients is all surpassed by the yogī. Knowing the truth established here, and becoming a yogī and knower, he reaches the supreme, primordial abode of Viṣṇu, the source of the world.
word_for_word: the determination of the meaning of the eight questions
through study and the like in the Vedas
through performance and the like in sacrifices
through austerities such as mortifying the body
through gifts such as offering to worthy recipients
having become a yogī and knower
which is the root of the world
